newsitem.title: USA: NFL-PATRIOTS ROOKIE GLENN PROVES "SHE" CAN PLAY.
newsitem.headline: NFL-PATRIOTS ROOKIE GLENN PROVES "SHE" CAN PLAY.

text.p: A tragic childhood and an unwelcoming head coach could not deter New England Patriots rookie receiver Terry Glenn from proving "she" could make it in the National Football League.

At the tender age of 22, Glenn, who never knew his father and whose mother was murdered when he was just 13, now stands poised to play in the Super Bowl as an integral part of the offence for a great coach who did not want him on the team.

New England coach Bill Parcells, who takes his team into Super Bowl XXXI against the Green Bay Packers on Sunday, made no secret of his displeaure when the Patriots drafted Glenn in the first round last year rather than select the defensive player he wanted.

Matters became even more tense when a hamstring injury forced Glenn to miss training camp, all of pre-season and the first game of the season. The injury led to a notorious crack by Parcells, who when asked how Glenn was doing quipped, "She's doing okay."
Glenn responded by winning over his sceptical coach on the field of battle, coming back to record an NFL rookie record 90 catches for 1,132 yards and six touchdowns.
"I see signs up in the stands now that say 'She Can Play'," the soft-spoken Glenn said with a laugh Wednesday.
Glenn insists now that he was too focused on healing and "getting my first taste of the NFL" to be bothered by "the she thing."

He also got support from running back Curtis Martin and quarterback Drew Bledsoe, who had had their share of being terrorised by Parcells. "Drew told me 'don't let Parcells get to you, he's trying to see how tough you are.'"

"(Parcells) knows that I'm going to play my hardest and give it my all and I know that if I go out and do that, I can please him," Glenn said of his highly-respected tormentor, who won two Super Bowls as coach of the New York Giants.
"Winning and going to the Super Bowl definitely cancelled out any kind of problems that we had in training camp."

Glenn said he finally won over Parcells with a stellar performance in the final game of the season, spearheading a come-from-behind road win over the Giants with eight catches for 124 yards and a crucial touchdown in a 23-22 victory.
"It was a very emotional game for him, he really wanted to win that game," Glenn said of Parcells, who hugged his rookie standout after the game, sharing a rare emotional moment.
But winning over Parcells was by no means the most difficult hurdle cleared by Glenn.
As an orphaned teenager Glenn sold sodas at $30 a tray at Ohio State football games in his hometown of Columbus.

"But I only sold like a half a tray because I was too busy watching the games," recalled Glenn, who went on to star as an All-American receiver for Ohio State after avoiding the pitfalls of life on the mean streets.
"Ever since the incident with my mother things have just worked out for me," he said.
Glenn said he could easily have ended up in jail "growing up in a rough neighbourhood, where your best friends like to do things that are bad things."
"But somehow God guided me to go play football."
Glenn said he had a healthy fear of getting into trouble.
"I didn't want to be locked up and not be able to take care of my little sister," added Glenn, who was forced to grow up a lot faster than most of his football playing peers.
Glenn has no desire to meet his father. "I don't have anything to say to him.
"I never had a father figure around the house....It was tough, it's tough now."
Glenn just marvels at the way his life seems to have worked out.
"My mother always harped on me about school, but I was too worried about sports. Nobody pushed me to play football, I did it on my own.
"I stuck with it for years and I wound up here -- in the Super Bowl."
